metadata.title: Cloud Architecture Patterns
metadata.description: Vendor-neutral architecture patterns for modern distributed systems
metadata.author: Mark Alexiuk

patterns.title: Asynchronous Job Processing
patterns.problem: A synchronous request invokes work whose duration, failure rate, or throughput cannot safely be handled within the request-response path. Waiting for completion can exhaust client connections, exceed request timeouts, or fail under load spikes.
patterns.decision: Accept the request durably into a queue, return immediately to the client, and process it asynchronously through a worker pool. Expose work status, retry behavior, and failure handling explicitly. The queue acts as a durable buffer and allows workers to scale independently.
use_when: Work duration is unpredictable or exceeds request timeouts
Retries and durable audit trails matter for compliance or reliability
You need to prioritize work, batch it, or distribute it across multiple workers
Multiple workers may process the same type of work in parallel
Decoupling producers from execution improves system resilience
avoid_when: Immediate synchronous confirmation is non-negotiable (e.g., payment authorization, form validation)
The operation is simple and always completes in milliseconds
The operational complexity and cost of queue infrastructure is unjustifiable for the workload
You have no mechanism to report completion status back to the client

tradeoffs.benefit: Decouples producers from workers; workers scale independently from request rate
tradeoffs.cost: Operational complexity: queue, worker pool, monitoring, dead-letter handling, idempotency logic

tradeoffs.benefit: Enables retries with backoff, durable record of work, and recovery from transient failures
tradeoffs.cost: Eventual consistency; client cannot immediately verify success; must poll or use webhooks

tradeoffs.benefit: Graceful degradation under load; queue absorbs spikes and workers process at their own pace
tradeoffs.cost: Requires idempotency design and duplicate-detection policy to avoid executing the same work twice

tradeoffs.benefit: Visibility into work status, failures, and processing time across the entire pipeline
tradeoffs.cost: Requires comprehensive logging and monitoring; operational alerts are essential

conceptual_components.label: Request API
conceptual_components.description: Accepts work requests, validates input, checks for duplicates, enqueues work

conceptual_components.label: Durable Queue
conceptual_components.description: Persists work durably; enables workers to pull tasks and guarantees no loss on producer failure

conceptual_components.label: Worker Pool
conceptual_components.description: Processes tasks; executes business logic, retries on transient failure, reports results

conceptual_components.label: Status/Result Store
conceptual_components.description: Persists work completion status and results; allows client to check progress or retrieve output

conceptual_components.label: Dead-Letter Queue
conceptual_components.description: Captures tasks that have failed after max retries; allows manual inspection and recovery

conceptual_components.label: Monitoring & Alerts
conceptual_components.description: Tracks queue depth, worker health, latency, error rates, and alerts on anomalies

diagram.alt: Client submits work through an API to a durable queue; workers claim tasks, execute them with retries, and update a status store. Failed tasks after max retries move to a dead-letter queue. Monitoring observes queue depth and worker health.

implementation_evidence.name: fleet-ops async worker framework
implementation_evidence.description: Task queue abstraction with retry logic, idempotency keys, status tracking, and dead-letter handling

implementation_evidence.name: fleet-base audit logger
implementation_evidence.description: Durable event log for async operations; serves as source of truth for retries and compliance audits

design_decisions.rationale: Work is persisted to queue before API returns to client; guarantees no loss on client disconnect or API failure
Requests with same ID are deduplicated; safe to retry without duplicate execution; critical for state mutations
Failed tasks are requeued with exponential backoff; transient failures resolve; max retries prevent infinite loops
Tasks that fail after max retries move to separate queue; allows human inspection, debugging, and manual recovery
Client can poll API for work status or subscribe to webhooks; no surprise failures or silent discards
Queue depth monitored; can reject new work if queue exceeds threshold; alerts if workers lag behind producers
Log task lifecycle (submitted, claimed, executed, completed, failed); trace correlation across components

variations.name: Push vs. Pull
variations.description: Workers pull tasks from queue (simpler, avoids thundering herd) vs. queue pushes to workers (lower latency, harder to backpressure)

variations.name: Ordering Guarantees
variations.description: FIFO (SQS, Redis) preserves order; topic subscriptions (Kafka) allow multiple consumers; best-effort has no guarantee

variations.name: Acknowledgment Model
variations.description: Explicit ack (worker confirms success before task is removed) vs. automatic ack (faster, but risk of loss)

variations.name: Visibility Timeout
variations.description: Task is invisible to other workers for a duration after being claimed; prevents concurrent execution; must extend if work takes longer

patterns.title: Strangler Fig: Incremental Legacy Modernization
patterns.problem: A legacy system is mission-critical but increasingly costly to maintain, lacks desired features, or blocks adoption of new technologies. A complete rewrite is too risky and blocks business value. You need to modernize incrementally while keeping the system live.
patterns.decision: Build a facade (strangler) that intercepts requests destined for the legacy system. Route specific feature requests to the new system, while others continue through to the legacy implementation. Over time, shift more traffic to the new system as capabilities are proven. The legacy system is gradually 'strangled' until it can be retired entirely.
use_when: The legacy system is stable, mission-critical, and cannot be taken offline
You can identify seams or boundaries—features or flows that can be migrated incrementally
The new system can coexist with the legacy system for a transition period
You have the organizational capacity to maintain two systems in parallel
Risk reduction and business continuity are higher priorities than speed
avoid_when: The entire system must be replaced simultaneously (regulatory deadline, hardware EOL)
The legacy system has deeply entangled logic with no clear seams
Operating two systems in parallel is infeasible (cost, complexity, skill constraints)
The legacy system is already isolated and easy to replace in one go

tradeoffs.benefit: Risk is spread across multiple deployments; each feature can be tested independently before full cutover
tradeoffs.cost: Operational complexity increases: need to run, monitor, and debug two systems in parallel for months

tradeoffs.benefit: Business value is delivered incrementally; users gain new capabilities while stability is maintained
tradeoffs.cost: Seam identification takes careful analysis; poor boundaries create cross-system dependencies and make migration harder

tradeoffs.benefit: Graceful fallback is possible; if the new system fails, traffic reverts to legacy without data loss
tradeoffs.cost: Requires robust routing/facade logic and data synchronization between systems

tradeoffs.benefit: Team can learn and iterate on new system design while legacy system handles baseline load
tradeoffs.cost: Legacy system must remain operational; cannot be abandoned immediately even after new system goes live

conceptual_components.label: Routing Facade
conceptual_components.description: Intercepts requests, decides routing based on feature flags, user cohorts, or request patterns

conceptual_components.label: New System (Capability X)
conceptual_components.description: Newly built system handling specific features or domains

conceptual_components.label: Legacy System
conceptual_components.description: Existing system; continues handling unmigrated features

conceptual_components.label: Data Bridge / Reconciliation
conceptual_components.description: Syncs data between new and legacy systems; ensures consistency for cross-system operations

conceptual_components.label: Monitoring & Feature Flags
conceptual_components.description: Tracks routing decisions, error rates, and controls cutover via feature flags

diagram.alt: Client requests route through a facade to either the new system (for enabled features) or legacy system (for everything else). Data bridge synchronizes state. Monitoring tracks routing and failures.

implementation_evidence.name: fleet-ops modernization router
implementation_evidence.description: Request routing based on feature flags; metrics on legacy vs. new system traffic

implementation_evidence.name: fleet-base audit logger
implementation_evidence.description: Durable event log for cross-system consistency; enables reconciliation and rollback

design_decisions.rationale: Identify feature boundaries or domain-driven slices that can be migrated independently; loose coupling between seams reduces migration friction
Use flags to control which users/requests go to new system; enables A/B testing and gradual rollout; quick rollback if issues arise
Sync state between old and new databases; ensures consistency if cross-system operations occur; may use event streaming or periodic reconciliation
If new system fails, requests revert to legacy; no user data loss; enables safe experimentation
Track routing decisions, latency, error rates in both systems; alerts on divergence or new system degradation
Plan a sunset date for legacy system; at cutover, retire legacy and data bridge; celebrate migration completion

variations.name: Routing Strategy
variations.description: Route by user cohort (canary, percentage), feature flag, request pattern, or domain; each has different risk/complexity profiles

variations.name: Data Synchronization
variations.description: Real-time event stream (Kafka), periodic batch sync, query-time joins, or read-through cache; affects consistency and latency

variations.name: Fallback Behavior
variations.description: Automatic fallback to legacy on new-system error, explicit user choice, or operator-controlled switch; affects user experience

variations.name: Scope of Replacement
variations.description: Replace one feature (micro), one domain (domain-driven), or one tier (API vs. backend); larger scopes are riskier but faster
